definition: Pruning is a data compression technique in machine learning and search algorithms that reduces the size of decision trees by removing sections of the tree that are non-critical and redundant to classify instances.
details: Pruning reduces the complexity of the final classifier, and hence improves predictive accuracy by the reduction of overfitting. One of the questions that arises in a decision tree algorithm is the optimal size of the final tree. A tree that is too large risks overfitting the training data and poorly generalizing to new samples. A small tree might not capture important structural information about the sample space. However, it is hard to tell when a tree algorithm should stop because it is impossible to tell if the addition of a single extra node will dramatically decrease error. This problem is known as the horizon effect. A common strategy is to grow the tree until each node contains a small number of instances then use pruning to remove nodes that do not provide additional information. Pruning should reduce the size of a learning tree without reducing predictive accuracy as measured by a cross-validation set. There are many techniques for tree pruning that differ in the measurement that is used to optimize performance.

explainer.lead: Decision tree pruning cuts away branches that add complexity without helping classification. It is a way to balance an oversized tree that memorizes training data against an undersized tree that misses useful structure, with the goal of better predictions on new samples.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a guessing game where you keep adding questions until every practice example is sorted perfectly. Some final questions may only separate one or two unusual examples, so you remove them and check that your guesses are still accurate. Pruning is that cleanup: keep the useful questions and drop the ones that do not help.
tiers.practitioner: A common workflow is to grow the tree until its nodes contain few instances, then remove nodes that add no useful information. Judge candidate prunes with a cross-validation set: the smaller tree should retain predictive accuracy. Choosing the stopping point directly is difficult because one more node could sharply reduce error, a problem called the horizon effect.
tiers.paperLevel: Given a learned decision tree, pruning selects a smaller subtree by removing non-critical or redundant sections, reducing classifier complexity and overfitting. A common requirement is that size decrease without lowering predictive accuracy measured on a cross-validation set. Pruning methods differ in the performance measurement they optimize, and an overly small tree can omit important structure in the sample space.

explainer.example: Suppose a customer tree ends with a branch that splits just two training customers by whether their postcode ends in an odd digit. If removing that split leaves cross-validation accuracy unchanged, pruning replaces the branch with its simpler parent prediction. The resulting tree is less tailored to those two customers and less complex.

explainer.intuition: A fully grown tree can contain very specific branches that fit quirks of the training data rather than general patterns. Pruning trims those branches back, aiming for the smallest tree that still classifies unseen instances well.
howItWorks: Grow a large tree until each node contains a small number of instances.
Identify nodes or sections whose removal loses no additional useful information.
Remove those sections to obtain a smaller tree.
Check predictive accuracy with a cross-validation set.
Keep pruning only while accuracy is not reduced.
explainer.whyItMatters: Pruning addresses the hard choice of final tree size: large trees risk overfitting, while small trees can miss important structure. It offers a way to simplify an already grown tree without sacrificing cross-validated predictive accuracy.
misconceptions: Pruning does not mean making the tree as small as possible.
A smaller training error is not the goal; pruning targets performance on new samples.
Pruning is not simply choosing an arbitrary stopping point before growth.
